newsitem.title: USA: NYC drops Corbin, no plans to pick new advisor.
newsitem.headline: NYC drops Corbin, no plans to pick new advisor.

text.p: New York City, which last month formally shut the door on financial advisor P.G. Corbin & Co, has no plans to replace the company, city sources said on Thursday.

P.G. Corbin was one of two financial advisors for the city, but New York City does not expect to pick another firm because the current advisor, Public Resources Advisory Group, gets good ratings, said the sources, who declined to be named.

The next opportunity for the city to hire another financial advisor is expected to arrive when a new infrastructure agency is authorized. A bill to create the new authority, which would be used to sidestep the city's constitutional debt limit, is being negotiated between the city comptroller and the Giuliani Administration, and the state would have to approve it.

Spokesmen for the comptroller, Alan Hevesi, who suspended P.G. Corbin on June 30, 1995, over a dispute over $5,000 in taxes that the city said the firm owed, explained that the comtroller waited to formalize a temination until he had received reports from city agencies investigating the matter.

The dispute had centered around New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani's desire to have only one firm market its bonds, while Hevesi had felt that using two firms would help ensure the city got the highest prices for its debt.

Hevesi also had wished to continue a policy begun under Mayor David Dinkins of encouraging businesses that were owned by minorities and women, but the new mayor felt appointments should be based strictly on merit, the sources recalled.

Robert Fink, an attorney for Corbin, which is led by Patricia Corbin, a black entrepreneuner, defended the advisor's work, saying it outperformed many of the more established companies that served the city before it was hired. The head of the firm, Patricia Corbin, was travelling and could not be reached for comment.
